articles.title: The Invisible Work of Keeping Detectives Equipped
articles.deck: An investigation into who replaces the batteries.
paragraphs: Every celebrated detective stands on the shoulders of someone who remembered to order evidence bags.
Our survey found that agents describe a working flashlight as "standard equipment" and a broken one as "a personal betrayal". Neither group could name the person who bought the batteries.

Before your next operation, check your kit, return what you borrowed, and thank the person at the counter. They cannot guarantee your survival. They can, however, stop you investigating a cellar with a stapler.
articles.prompt: Show Alex the article about equipment staff.

lines: They interviewed thirty detectives before discovering batteries come from somewhere. Outstanding investigative work.
People remember who signed out the gun. Nobody remembers who checked the torch, replaced the strap and found the missing charger.
You read the bit about returning things? Good. Keep that part. You can underline it.
recall: Still got that article? Good. Every time you return something with all its pieces, I consider it a favourable review.

articles.title: Your Filing System May Be a Cry for Help
articles.deck: The floor is not an archive. We checked.
paragraphs: There are three popular filing systems: alphabetical, chronological, and "I saw it here a minute ago".
The third system offers excellent exercise and poor results in court. Experts recommend putting a date on documents, keeping versions distinct, and resisting the urge to label every folder FINAL.
If a colleague asks whether you have seen a missing report, "Define missing" is not considered a constructive response.
articles.prompt: Ask Alex about the filing article.

lines: A magazine has finally discovered folders. Next month: shelves.
My inventory is filed. The things people insist they already returned are filed separately. Under "No".
recall: The floor is still not an archive. I am pleased the magazine and I remain in agreement.

articles.title: Twelve Coats You Cannot Afford
articles.deck: Dress for the case you want. Expense the coat you actually own.
paragraphs: This season, the discerning detective is wearing charcoal, regret, and a price tag facing inward.
Our premium model includes a storm flap, secret pockets, and the confidence of someone who has never submitted an expense claim.
Budget alternative: keep your current coat. Turn up the collar. Look as if the weather owes you money.

lines: That one costs more than the shelving. The shelving holds more detectives' belongings and complains less.
Buy whatever coat you like. I am not issuing a replacement because the first one went out of fashion.
recall: Did you buy the coat? No? Sensible. It still would not count as a field kit.
